data.title: User Story
data.tagline: A brief requirement that states who needs what and why from the user's perspective
data.learningOutcome: You can turn a feature idea into a user story with a user, goal, and reason, then identify the acceptance criteria and business rules still missing.
data.description: A traveler may need to save an unfinished itinerary so they can continue on another device. A user story starts a requirements conversation but does not replace interaction details, acceptance criteria, or technical design.

learning.assumes: You have seen feature requests such as “add a save button” without a clear user or problem.
learning.outcome: You can turn a feature idea into a user story with a user, goal, and reason, then identify the acceptance criteria and business rules still missing.

explanation.title: Name a specific user
explanation.text: Describe the person and situation instead of hiding different needs behind “all users.”

explanation.title: Replace the feature label with a goal
explanation.text: A save button is a solution; continuing an unfinished itinerary later is the result the user needs.

explanation.title: Add checkable conditions separately
explanation.text: Keep the story brief, then put scope, exceptions, and completion conditions in Acceptance Criteria or a Use Case.

data.boundary: A User Story starts the conversation. A Use Case describes the interaction, while Acceptance Criteria state what the result must satisfy.

lessonPractice.title: A team plans to add trip saving. Which option works best as a user story?

options.label: As a traveler planning a multi-day trip, I want to save an unfinished itinerary so I can continue editing it later
options.feedback: Correct. It names the user, goal, and value, giving the team a useful starting point for discussing scope and acceptance criteria.

options.label: Add a saveTrip() method, a database table, and a blue button in the top right
options.feedback: That is an implementation and interface list. It does not explain who needs the feature or why.

options.label: Add a better trip-saving experience
options.feedback: That is only a feature label with a vague quality claim. It does not identify the user, goal, or value.

data.agentPrompt: Turn “save a trip” into a user story that states the target user, goal, and reason. Use only the facts I provide, and list unsupported user claims or business rules as open questions. Then add directly checkable acceptance criteria without deciding the button position or database structure.
